name: The Standard of Taste
statement: Is there any objective standard for judgments of beauty, or is taste merely subjective?
statementAccent: any objective standard for judgments of beauty
meaning: The problem of taste, or the standard of taste, concerns whether there is any objective standard for judgments of beauty and aesthetic value, given the apparent subjectivity of taste. Aesthetic judgments seem to be based on subjective feeling or pleasure, captured in the sayings that there is no disputing about taste, yet we also argue about them, defer to critics and experts, and hold that some judgments are better than others. So are aesthetic judgments merely subjective, or is there a standard of taste? David Hume, in his 1757 essay Of the Standard of Taste, from his Four Dissertations, acknowledged that taste is based on sentiment rather than reason, which seems to point toward relativism, since in one sense all sentiment is right; yet he argued that there is a standard, found not in a rule or definition but in the joint verdict of qualified true judges, or ideal critics. The qualities of a good critic, on Hume's account, are delicacy of taste or sentiment, illustrated by the wine-tasting story from Don Quixote in which two kinsmen detect faint traces of leather and iron later traced to a key with a leathern thong at the bottom of the cask; practice; comparison across many works; freedom from prejudice; and good sense. Immanuel Kant took a different route, holding that the judgment of taste is subjective, based on feeling, yet claims universal validity, an antinomy grounded in the free play of imagination and understanding and a presumed common sense.
mechanism: The problem arises from a tension in aesthetic judgment. On one side, calling something beautiful expresses a felt response, a pleasure or sentiment, and sentiments do not seem to be true or false in the way factual judgments are, which suggests that in matters of taste each person's response is simply their own and there can be no error or standard. On the other side, we treat aesthetic judgments as more than arbitrary: we argue about them, revise them, recognize expertise, and hold that the judgment that a great work is trivial is worse than the judgment that it is great. Hume resolves the tension without abandoning the basis of taste in sentiment. He grants that beauty is not a property in objects but a sentiment in the mind, so that no rule or definition can dictate taste; but he argues that some sentiments are the product of better-functioning critical faculties than others, and that the standard of taste lies in the joint verdict of critics who possess the requisite qualities. Such a true judge has delicacy, the sensitivity to detect fine qualities that coarser palates miss, as the wine-tasters detected the leather and the iron; practice in the relevant art; wide comparison of works, which alone lets one rank them; freedom from prejudice, so that irrelevant biases do not distort the response; and good sense to grasp a work's design. The verdicts of such qualified critics, wherever they may be found, constitute the true standard of taste and beauty, though Hume allows that two sources of blameless variation remain, differences of temperament among individuals and differences of culture across ages. Kant grounds the normativity of taste differently, in a subjective universality: the judgment of taste, though based on disinterested pleasure and not on concepts, demands the agreement of everyone, presupposing a common sense.

For Kant the judgment of taste is subjective yet demands universal agreement, as if beauty were a property of the object.

whyItMatters: The standard of taste is one of the foundational problems of aesthetics, because it asks whether judgments of beauty and artistic value can be right or wrong, or are merely expressions of personal preference. The stakes are high: if there is no standard of taste, then criticism, expertise, artistic canons, and the very idea that some works are better than others lose their footing; if there is a standard, we must say what it is and how it can be reconciled with the evident basis of taste in feeling. Hume's essay Of the Standard of Taste is the classic attempt to thread this needle, granting that beauty lies in sentiment yet grounding an objective standard in the joint verdict of qualified critics, and his account of the true judge, delicacy, practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice, and good sense, remains the touchstone for thinking about critical authority and the education of taste. Kant's alternative, that the judgment of taste is subjectively grounded yet lays claim to universal agreement, is one of the deepest treatments of the peculiar normativity of aesthetic judgment. The problem bears on the role of critics, the possibility of aesthetic progress, and the objectivity of value generally.

working.text: acknowledge that judgments of beauty rest on sentiment or pleasure, not on rules or reason.
with Hume, locate the standard of taste in the joint verdict of qualified true judges.
require delicacy, practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice, and good sense in a good critic.

limits: The standard of taste is a problem rather than a solved question, and Hume's solution faces objections. A central worry is circularity or regress: Hume identifies the standard with the verdict of true judges, but the marks of a true judge, delicacy, good sense, and the rest, seem to be specified partly by their tending to agree in their verdicts, so it can seem that we identify good critics by their good judgments and good judgments by their being made by good critics, without an independent standard. There is also the question of how far Hume's account really secures objectivity, given that he concedes two sources of blameless variation, individual temperament and cultural difference across ages, which limit the reach of any universal standard. Kant's alternative, that the judgment of taste is subjective yet universally valid, is powerful but obscure, and how a merely subjective ground could license a demand for everyone's agreement is much debated, the antinomy of taste. Hume's essay appeared in 1757 in the Four Dissertations, the wine story derives from Don Quixote, and Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment dates to 1790.
misreadings: The problem of taste is not settled by the slogan that there is no disputing about taste, since we do dispute about it and defer to critics, which is what makes the problem live. Hume's standard is not a rule or definition of beauty but the joint verdict of qualified critics, and it does not deny that taste rests on sentiment. And Kant's view is not that beauty is an objective property, but that a subjectively grounded judgment nonetheless claims universal validity, so treating the problem as closed by relativism, Hume's standard as a rule, or Kant's as making beauty objective, misreads the debate.
origin: The problem of whether there is an objective standard for judgments of beauty, given the subjectivity of taste, addressed by Hume's Of the Standard of Taste (1757) via the joint verdict of true judges and by Kant's account of the judgment of taste.
